claims.text: The initial material is a single-phase CoFeNiCr high-entropy alloy.
The initial alloy has a typical grain size of tens of micrometers.
Adding 3–5 atomic % Dy to CoFeNiCr will increase its coercive field relative to an undoped matched baseline.
Dy addition will produce Dy-rich clusters or local chemical inhomogeneities.
Dy-rich regions will enhance local magnetocrystalline anisotropy.
Dy-rich clusters or local chemical inhomogeneities will elevate energy barriers for domain-wall motion.
Enhanced magnetocrystalline anisotropy in Dy-rich regions will hinder domain-wall movement.
Hindered domain-wall movement will raise the coercive field.
Under identical annealing at approximately 900 K for 2 hours in vacuum, 3–5 atomic % Dy will increase coercive field by 20–30% relative to undoped CoFeNiCr.
Identical annealing of the baseline and Dy-doped samples will ensure uniform microstructure and composition.
Dy concentrations above approximately 8 atomic % could cause second-phase formation or other microstructural changes.
Second-phase formation or other microstructural changes above approximately 8 atomic % Dy could mitigate or reverse the coercivity increase.
The optimal Dy doping level for coercivity is not well established and may depend on processing and alloy formulation.

contradictions.description: The conditions state that annealing is intended to ensure uniform composition, whereas the proposed mediator requires Dy-rich clusters or local chemical inhomogeneities.

The proposed mechanism requires Dy-rich regions or chemical inhomogeneity, but the experiment seeks to confirm uniform Dy distribution without specifying a length scale that would reconcile uniform mapping with nanoscale clustering.

The prediction is a 20–30% coercivity increase, but the hypothesis is only falsified below a statistically significant 5% increase; an increase between 5% and 20% would contradict the quantified prediction without meeting the stated falsification rule.
